Only sumatriptan/naproxen sodium was associated with a significantly higher OR compared with placebo for pain freedom from two to 24 h (OR: 2.31, 95% CI: 1.31-4.07). Ibuprofen exhibited the highest effect size for pain relief at 2 hours (OR: 3.21, 95% CI: 1.10-9.34). None of the included drugs was found to reduce the use of rescue drugs from two to 24 h. Zolmitriptan was associated with the highest risk of AEs among all treatments. Acetaminophen appears to have the lowest risk of adverse events, comparable to that of a placebo.

Conclusion

Ibuprofen can effectively relieve symptoms, characterized by a favorable benefit-risk profile. Sumatriptan and zolmitriptan nasal sprays also exhibited robust efficacy, specifically among populations with prominent nausea and vomiting. Sumatriptan/naproxen sodium merits consideration, especially in patients exhibiting an inadequate response to monotherapy. Dihydroergotamine demonstrated potential benefits in refractory and chronic migraine; however, high-quality studies are warranted to validate these findings.

records.title: Global Trends in Integrating Machine Learning (ML) with Model-Informed Drug Development (MIDD): A Bibliometric and Systematic Review (2015-2025).

content.title: Global Trends in Integrating Machine Learning (ML) with Model-Informed Drug Development (MIDD): A Bibliometric and Systematic Review (2015-2025).
content.abstract: Background/Objectives: The integration of machine learning (ML) within model-informed drug development (MIDD) represents a rapidly evolving paradigm in pharmacometrics, enabling improved prediction, optimization, and regulatory decision-making across drug development pipelines. However, the extent to which ML methods are explicitly integrated into regulatory decision-making remains limited and unevenly characterized. This study aims to systematically map the ML-MIDD scholarly landscape, identify core sources and contributors, assess thematic evolution, and summarize key methodological advancements through an integrative bibliometric and systematic review. Methods: A comprehensive literature search was conducted across Web of Science, Scopus, and PubMed (2015-2025), followed by metadata harmonization and deduplication. Bibliometric analysis was performed using Bibliometrix, VOSviewer, and PRISMA guidelines to characterize publication trends, collaboration patterns, thematic structures, and representative methodological contributions. Results: A total of 770 records were initially retrieved, with Scopus contributing the largest share (n = 343; 44.5%), followed by Web of Science (n = 322; 41.8%) and PubMed (n = 105; 13.6%). After deduplication, 607 unique publications remained (78.8% of total), and 560 were included in the final systematic review (97.6% of full texts). Publications spanned 269 sources, with core journals accounting for 28% of output. The United States led in volume (n = 665; 20.8%) and international collaboration (16.47%). Thematic evolution revealed transitions from foundational PK/PD methods (2016-2018) to applied ML-driven precision pharmacology (2022-2025). Conclusions: Emerging methods included deep learning, reinforcement learning, and hybrid mechanistic-ML models. ML-MIDD is a rapidly maturing interdisciplinary field, evidenced by expanding methodological diversity and increasing use of ML-enabled components within regulatory-relevant modeling workflows, rather than formal regulatory endorsement of ML-MIDD as a standalone methodology, indicating growing translational relevance but continued need for validation and regulatory clarity.

records.title: Global meta-analysis unravels mechanistic shifts in plant growth and physiological adaptability under nitrogen dioxide modulation.

content.title: Global meta-analysis unravels mechanistic shifts in plant growth and physiological adaptability under nitrogen dioxide modulation.
content.abstract: Quantitatively elucidating plant responses to elevated nitrogen dioxide (eNO<sub>2</sub>) is essential for understanding global atmospheric nitrogen pollution and ecosystem nitrogen cycling, yet a comprehensive synthesis is still lacking. Here, we integrated data from 80 independent experiments worldwide and conducted a multivariate mixed-effects meta-analysis to evaluate the effects of eNO<sub>2</sub> on 73 plant traits encompassing growth, physiology, and biochemistry. Overall, eNO<sub>2</sub> significantly reduced plant growth performance and diminished environmental adaptability by disrupting water regulation, photosynthesis, mineral nutrient uptake, and hormone-mediated processes. Subgroup analyses based on the between-group heterogeneity (Q<sub>B</sub>) statistic revealed that plant functional types were major determinants of response variability; specifically, clonal, herbaceous, deciduous, and C<sub>3</sub> species exhibited greater sensitivity to eNO<sub>2</sub>. Linear and nonlinear dose-response analyses, including restricted cubic spline (RCS) models, further demonstrated that plant responses were jointly shaped by exposure concentration and duration, and that chronic low-level eNO<sub>2</sub> could induce growth stimulation resembling hormone-like regulatory effects. Collectively, this study provides the comprehensive quantitative framework for understanding plant responses to eNO<sub>2</sub>, offering critical insights into the mechanisms underlying plant adaptation to atmospheric nitrogen pollution and informing the design of nitrogen-cycle manipulation experiments.

records.title: Effects of Traditional and Technology-Based Exercise Interventions on Cognitive Function in Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

content.title: Effects of Traditional and Technology-Based Exercise Interventions on Cognitive Function in Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

As population aging accelerates, pharmacological treatments provide limited benefits for cognitive decline. Exercise and technology-assisted exercise have thus emerged as important non-pharmacological approaches for supporting cognitive health in older adults. However, comparative evidence on the relative effectiveness of different intervention modalities across cognitive outcomes remains limited.

Objective

This study used a network meta-analysis to systematically compare and rank the effects of traditional and non-traditional exercise interventions on cognitive function in older adults.

Methods

This systematic review and network meta-analysis was registered on PROSPERO (CRD420261278685). PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched from inception to May 2026. Randomized controlled trials enrolling participants aged 60 years or older were included. Interventions comprised aerobic, resistance, mind-body, finger, and multicomponent exercise, as well as virtual reality-based interventions, artificial intelligence-assisted exercise, and wearable exoskeleton training. Primary outcomes included global cognition, executive function, memory, attention, and activities of daily living. A random effects network meta-analysis was applied to estimate standardized mean differences with 95 percent confidence intervals, and intervention rankings were derived using SUCRA values.

Results

A total of 70 randomized controlled trials involving 5573 older adults were included. All active interventions demonstrated overall cognitive benefits compared with usual care or non-active control conditions. Mind-body exercise showed the highest probability of improving global cognitive performance. Virtual reality-based interventions were particularly effective for executive function, memory, and activities of daily living, while artificial intelligence-assisted exercise showed favorable rankings for attention outcomes. Mind-body exercise showed favorable effects on global cognition, whereas several technology-assisted interventions ranked highly for selected cognitive and functional outcomes.

Conclusions

Both traditional and non non-traditional exercise interventions improve cognitive function in older adults, although their effects differ across cognitive domains. Technology-assisted approaches appear more effective for enhancing specific cognitive functions, while traditional interventions such as mind-body exercise are more advantageous for preserving overall cognitive performance. These findings highlight the potential value of stage specific and combined intervention strategies for promoting cognitive health in aging populations.

records.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of physical rehabilitation on functional recovery in critically ill patients.

content.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of physical rehabilitation on functional recovery in critically ill patients.
content.abstract:
Purpose

Survivors of critical illness frequently experience persistent physical impairment, particularly ICU-acquired weakness (ICU-AW), which contributes to prolonged disability after intensive care. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the effects of physical rehabilitation on muscle strength, physical function, health-related quality of life, and clinical outcomes in critically ill adults.

Methods

Four electronic databases were searched from inception to March 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing physical rehabilitation with usual rehabilitation in adult critically ill patients were included. The primary outcome was muscle strength assessed by the Medical Research Council (MRC) sum score. Secondary outcomes included ICU-AW, physical function, health-related quality of life, duration of mechanical ventilation (MV), mortality, and ICU and hospital length of stay.

Results

Forty RCTs involving 5,135 patients (2,554 physical rehabilitation; 2,581 usual rehabilitation) were included. Physical rehabilitation was associated with improved MRC sum score (SMD 0.26, 95% CI 0.05-0.46; p = 0.02; I 2 = 70%), reduced incidence of ICU-AW (OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.43-0.87; p = 0.007; I 2 = 34%), improved Barthel Index (SMD 0.62, 95% CI 0.21-1.03; p = 0.003; I 2 = 85%) and SF-36 physical function (SMD 0.53, 95% CI 0.26-0.81; p < 0.001; I 2 = 81%), shortened duration of MV (MD -1.32 days, 95% CI -1.98 to -0.65; p < 0.001; I 2 = 66%) and ICU length of stay (MD -1.41 days, 95% CI -2.03 to -0.78; p < 0.001; I 2 = 44%), but had no significant effects on mortality or hospital length of stay.

Conclusion

Physical rehabilitation is associated with improved muscle strength and functional recovery, reduced ICU-AW, and shorter mechanical ventilation duration and ICU stay, but not reduced mortality. Further high-quality Multicenter trials are needed to define the optimal rehabilitation strategy.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42023462649, Identifier CRD42023462649.

records.title: Global research trends and hotspots in human immunodeficiency virus-associated cervical cancer (1990-2025): a multi-database bibliometric analysis.

content.title: Global research trends and hotspots in human immunodeficiency virus-associated cervical cancer (1990-2025): a multi-database bibliometric analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Research on cervical cancer among WLWH represents a critical area for advancing long-term prevention and clinical management strategies. Yet as the volume of published literature in this field continues to grow rapidly, synthesizing and appraising the available evidence in a comprehensive manner has become increasingly challenging.

Objective

This study aims to map the global research landscape, identify leading contributors and collaborative networks, and delineate the knowledge base and emerging research priorities in HIV-associated cervical cancer through a bibliometric analysis of multiple databases. Particular attention is given to the molecular and immunological mechanisms underlying the synergistic oncogenic interaction between HIV and high-risk HPV, as well as current trends in translational clinical research.

Methods

Publications on HIV and cervical cancer from January 1, 1990, to December 31, 2025 (n = 6,137) were retrieved and analyzed using bibliometric and visualization tools, including R (bibliometrix), Python, VOSviewer, and CiteSpace. Analyses encompassed publication trends, collaboration networks, keyword co-occurrence, and thematic evolution.

Results

Research output has increased steadily, led by the United States, followed by China, South Africa, India, and the United Kingdom. The most productive journals include International Journal of Cancer and AIDS, which are also among the most frequently cited. The seminal reference is "Cancer-related Inflammation." Emerging research frontiers center on cervical cancer screening, WLWH, human papillomavirus vaccination, and deep learning.

Conclusions

Future directions will likely emphasize lifecycle vaccination strategies for WLWH, precision therapies guided by the immune microenvironment, and scalable screening approaches for low-resource settings. These findings provide evidence-based insights to inform global health policy and accelerate cervical cancer elimination efforts.

records.title: Beyond western paradigms: a cross-cultural review of social-emotional competence frameworks and the promise of AI-driven assessment.

content.title: Beyond western paradigms: a cross-cultural review of social-emotional competence frameworks and the promise of AI-driven assessment.
content.abstract:
Background

Social-emotional competence (SEC) is a critical yet culturally embedded construct. While foundational frameworks like collaborative for academic, social, and emotional learning (CASEL) and OECD provide influential models, their cross-cultural applicability and the validity of associated assessments are increasingly questioned, particularly in non-Western contexts. Concurrently, artificial intelligence (AI) presents novel opportunities for culturally responsive SEC measurement.

Objective

This systematic review synthesizes literature on the conceptualizations, theoretical frameworks, and measurement tools for adolescent SEC across diverse cultural settings, with a specific focus on the role of emerging digital technologies.

Methods

Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a comprehensive search of Web of Science and Google Scholar (2000-2025) was conducted. After AI-assisted triage and manual screening, 89 studies were included. A narrative synthesis was performed, employing thematic analysis to compare frameworks (e.g., CASEL, OECD, Chinese, Australian/New Zealand models) across theoretical foundations, operational dimensions, and measurement approaches.

Results

The analysis reveals that dominant SEC frameworks are cultural artifacts reflecting underlying individualist or collectivist values, leading to divergent prioritizations of competencies (e.g., autonomy vs. harmony). Achieving cross-cultural measurement invariance for standardized tools remains a significant challenge, necessitating strategies like anchoring vignettes and emic-etic integration. The review identifies a clear trajectory toward technology-enhanced assessment, highlighting the potential of multimodal AI analysis, generative AI for stimuli creation, virtual reality simulations, and large language models to enable more ecologically valid, behavioral, and culturally configurable evaluations. However, these technologies introduce risks of algorithmic bias and digital colonialism.

Conclusion

Advancing the field requires a pluralistic, dialogical approach that decentralizes Western models, invests in indigenous theory-building, and ethically harnesses technology. Future research must develop assessment methodologies that balance generalizability with deep cultural respect, leveraging AI as a tool for empowerment and context-rich insight rather than for imposing reductionist, cross-cultural rankings.

records.title: Artificial intelligence in the diagnosis of deep vein thrombosis: A scoping review.

content.title: Artificial intelligence in the diagnosis of deep vein thrombosis: A scoping review.
content.abstract: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is the formation of thrombi in the deep venous system, most often in the lower extremities. Although usually not life-threatening, DVT requires timely diagnosis to prevent complications such as pulmonary embolism and post-thrombotic syndrome. The growing demand for image interpretation has generated interest in applying artificial intelligence (AI) to automated DVT detection. This scoping review analyzes the performance of artificial intelligence in diagnosing DVT using computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and ultrasound (US). We conducted a search across seven databases from inception to May 2025 using terms related to deep vein thrombosis, artificial intelligence, and machine learning. Eligible studies were limited to those evaluating DVT diagnosis using CT, MRI, or ultrasound. Two independent reviewers selected eligible studies, and quality was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (QUADAS-2). Eleven studies published between 2021 and 2025 met the inclusion criteria. Some of the AI algorithms included RetinaNet, Deep R-Belief Neural Networks, and Sooty Tern Optimization. US-based models were the most studied algorithms, with sensitivities and specificities ranging from 68 to 100% and 70-100%, respectively. The MRI-based model achieved sensitivities, specificities, and accuracies of 95% to 97%. One CT-based model demonstrated a sensitivity of 83%. Studies evaluated across multiple imaging datasets showed high sensitivities, specificities, and precision of 96% or higher. Future research should prioritize multicenter validation and integration of clinical factors. In addition, explainable frameworks capable of integrating multiple imaging datasets must be developed with attention to workflow efficiency and cost-effectiveness to support clinical translation. The results indicate that AI is best situated as a supplementary tool rather than a replacement for expert interpretation in DVT diagnosis.

records.title: Association between prediabetes and the risk of atrial fibrillation: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Association between prediabetes and the risk of atrial fibrillation: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and a major contributor to morbidity and mortality. Although diabetes is a well-established risk factor for AF, the role of prediabetes-a modifiable metabolic condition-remains uncertain. Clarifying this relationship may help identify individuals at risk and guide early preventive strategies.

Methods

We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies identified through PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science databases up to November 21, 2025. Studies reporting adjusted hazard ratios for incident AF in adults with prediabetes compared with normoglycemic controls were included. Pooled estimates were calculated using random-effects models, and heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic. Prespecified subgroup analyses explored variations by definition of prediabetes, geographic region, follow-up duration, age, and sex. Publication bias was evaluated using Egger's and Begg's tests.

Results

Twelve independent datasets from 11 cohort studies, including over 15 million participants and 277,164 incident AF cases, were analyzed. Prediabetes was associated with a modest but statistically significant increased risk of AF (pooled hazard ratio: 1.20; 95% confidence interval: 1.08-1.35), with substantial heterogeneity. Sensitivity analyses showed consistent results. Subgroup analyses indicated a numerically stronger association in Asian populations than in Europe and North America; this finding should be interpreted cautiously given heterogeneity and limited studies per subgroup. Other subgroup analyses were broadly consistent, and overall evidence of publication bias was limited.

Conclusion

Prediabetes is associated with increased AF risk across diverse populations. Given the observational design, these findings indicate association rather than causation. Early identification and management of prediabetes may provide an opportunity for AF prevention.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/, identifier CRD420251233423.

records.title: Progress in pharmacovigilance research based on artificial intelligence and real-world data: a structured narrative review.

content.title: Progress in pharmacovigilance research based on artificial intelligence and real-world data: a structured narrative review.
content.abstract:
Background

Traditional pharmacovigilance (PV) relies heavily on spontaneous reporting systems (SRS), which remain vulnerable to under-reporting and limited mechanistic insight. Artificial intelligence (AI) and real-world data (RWD) offer opportunities to strengthen signal detection, risk prediction, and translational safety assessment, but most applications remain at retrospective development or early implementation stages.

Methods

We conducted a structured narrative scoping review with critical appraisal, reported using PRISMA-ScR. Literature from 2010 to 2026 was identified through expert review, reference chaining, and regulatory sources. English-language publications on AI or machine learning in clinical pharmacovigilance with real-world data were synthesized thematically across data sources, analytical methods, validation strategies, and implementation challenges.

Results

RWD ecosystems-including electronic health records (EHRs), administrative claims, multi-omics, and global SRS-can be integrated with supervised ML, natural language processing (NLP), graph neural networks (GNNs), and federated learning (FL) for diverse PV tasks. Reported area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) values often exceed 0.90 in internal validation, yet external validation, calibration, decision-curve analysis, and prospective implementation evidence remain inconsistently reported. Common data models such as the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) Common Data Model (CDM) and FL architectures improve interoperability and privacy-preserving collaboration. Causal and explainable AI methods are emerging but require explicit assumptions and mechanistic confirmation before regulatory-grade causal claims.

Conclusions

AI-enabled PV is transitioning from association-focused surveillance toward prediction, mechanistic interpretation, and implementation science, yet widespread clinical or regulatory adoption requires transparent reporting (e.g., TRIPOD + AI, PROBAST), rigorous external and prospective validation, clear separation of association from causation, clinically interpretable outputs, sustained human oversight, and governance within harmonizing regulatory frameworks.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Physical Therapy Interventions for Non-Specific Low Back Pain: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomised Controlled Trials.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Physical Therapy Interventions for Non-Specific Low Back Pain: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomised Controlled Trials.
content.abstract: Background/Objectives: Non-specific low back pain (NSLBP) is the leading cause of disability worldwide. Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly being integrated into healthcare interventions for NSLBP, yet their effectiveness remains uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of AI-based Physical therapy (PT) interventions on pain intensity and disability outcomes in patients with NSLBP. Methods: We conducted a comprehensive search across six electronic databases. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating AI-based interventions for NSLBP were only included. Mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using random-effects models. Heterogeneity was assessed using I2 statistics and Cochran's Q test. Results: Five RCTs (n = 1939) met the inclusion criteria for systematic review. Three RCTs (n = 594 participants) provided data for meta-analysis. AI-based interventions significantly reduced pain (pooled MD -0.721, 95% CI -1.047 to -0.395; z = -4.34, p < 0.001; I2 = 9.5%). Disability also significantly improved (pooled MD -1.031, 95% CI -2.020 to -0.042; t(2) = -4.48, p = 0.046; I2 = 0%). Neither effect reached the minimal clinically important difference (1.0 for pain, 2-4 for disability). No serious adverse events were reported. Conclusions: AI-based PT interventions produce statistically significant but clinically small improvements in pain and disability for NSLBP. Certainty of evidence is low due to risk of bias and imprecision. Larger, blinded RCTs with standardised outcomes are needed.

records.title: From graph models to intelligent decision-making: a review of spatio-temporal graph neural networks for regional disease risk prediction and etiology mining.

content.title: From graph models to intelligent decision-making: a review of spatio-temporal graph neural networks for regional disease risk prediction and etiology mining.
content.abstract:
Background

Regional disease risk prediction is a core component of public health early warning systems. Traditional statistical models and machine learning methods have inherent limitations in handling multi-source heterogeneous data fusion, complex spatio-temporal dependency modeling, and interpretable etiology mining, making it difficult to meet the demands of precise and real-time public health decision-making.

Objective

This review systematically examines the methodological advances, application scenarios, and future directions of spatio-temporal graph neural networks (ST-GNNs) and multi-source data fusion techniques in regional disease risk prediction and etiology mining, aiming to provide a bridging reference that connects cutting-edge technologies with practical applications for public health researchers, policymakers, and data scientists.

Methods

Following the PRISMA framework, we systematically searched the Web of Science, PubMed, and IEEE Xplore databases for the period 2023-2026, ultimately including 76 core studies. A four-layer methodological framework encompassing graph construction, fusion strategies, spatio-temporal modeling, and interpretable etiology mining was developed.

Results

Representative works are reviewed from two dimensions: prediction tasks (single-disease prediction, multi-disease collaborative forecasting, long-term extrapolation) and etiology mining (spatial transmission tracing, temporal pattern attribution, multi-factor interaction analysis). Five major technical challenges are identified: dynamic graph structure modeling, cross-modal heterogeneous fusion, trade-off between prediction and interpretability, out-of-distribution generalization, and privacy-preserving federated learning. These are complemented by implementation constraints from public health practice, including data availability, computational efficiency, and policy coordination.

Conclusion

The main contribution of this review is the construction of a unified methodological framework integrating prediction and etiology mining, and a systematic synthesis of the challenges and future pathways at the frontier of technology and practical implementation. ST-GNNs demonstrate significant advantages in improving prediction accuracy and interpretability. Future developments should deeply integrate foundation models and causal inference to build a "prediction-intervention-evaluation" closed-loop system, providing actionable methodological references for building regional disease early warning systems and formulating public health intervention strategies globally, especially in low- and middle-income regions, thereby enhancing public health emergency response capacity and health equity.

records.title: Safety profile of small interfering RNA therapeutics: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
records.publisher: Frontiers in drug safety and regulation

content.title: Safety profile of small interfering RNA therapeutics: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
content.abstract:
Objectives

Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) represent a promising therapeutic platform addressing unmet clinical needs. Recent advances have improved siRNA design, stability, specificity, and delivery; however, translating preclinical findings into clinical practice remains challenging due to the lack of standardized safety evaluation frameworks. This study conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of placebo-controlled randomized clinical trials (RCTs) to quantitatively assess the safety of siRNA therapeutics and evaluate the adequacy of current preclinical safety assessments.

Methods

PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane databases were searched from inception to July 2025. Two reviewers independently performed study selection and data extraction according to predefined criteria. Safety outcomes included death, serious adverse events (SAEs), severe adverse events, and adverse events (AEs) leading to treatment discontinuation. Pooled relative risks (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using R packages meta and metafor. Methodological quality for AE assessment was evaluated using the McHarm scale. The protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251120555).

Results

Of 5,527 records screened, 57 studies (53 reports) evaluating 28 siRNA agents were included. Compared with controls, siRNA treatment did not increase the risk of death (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.62-0.95) and severe AEs (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.76-0.95), with no statistical heterogeneity (I2 = 0%). Risks of SAEs (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.88-1.00) and treatment discontinuation (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.66-1.13) were not increased.

Conclusion

Chemical and delivery advancements have effectively enhanced siRNA safety. Nevertheless, ongoing vigilance and comprehensive safety monitoring during early clinical phases remain essential to identify unforeseen toxicities.

Systematic review registration

Identifier CRD420251120555.

records.title: Endoscopic Diagnosis of Chronic Atrophic Gastritis and Early Gastric Cancer: From Basics to Advanced Imaging.

content.title: Endoscopic Diagnosis of Chronic Atrophic Gastritis and Early Gastric Cancer: From Basics to Advanced Imaging.
content.abstract: Chronic atrophic gastritis (CAG) is the principal precursor lesion for gastric adenocarcinoma and represents a key target for endoscopic surveillance and early intervention. Although the global age-standardised incidence of gastric cancer has declined over recent decades, the absolute number of cases continues to rise because of population ageing and increasing incidence in younger individuals. The prognosis remains poor in advanced disease, whereas early gastric cancer (EGC) detected at a mucosal stage is associated with excellent long-term survival and may be curable with endoscopic resection. Consequently, high-quality endoscopic detection of premalignant gastric lesions is essential to reduce gastric cancer mortality. This review summarises current concepts in the endoscopic diagnosis of CAG, gastric intestinal metaplasia (GIM), and EGC, from conventional white-light endoscopy through to advanced imaging and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted systems. Fundamental principles of high-quality oesophagogastroduodenoscopy are discussed, including adequate inspection time, systematic mucosal assessment, mucosal cleansing, and standardised photo-documentation. Characteristic endoscopic appearances of normal gastric mucosa, atrophy, and intestinal metaplasia are reviewed, alongside established staging systems including the Kimura-Takemoto and EGGIM classifications. The role of image-enhanced endoscopy is examined in detail, including narrow-band imaging, linked colour imaging, texture and colour enhancement imaging, and magnification optical enhancement. These modalities improve visualisation of pit patterns, microvascular architecture, and hallmark features of intestinal metaplasia such as the light blue crest sign, substantially increasing diagnostic sensitivity and specificity compared with conventional white light imaging alone. Advanced imaging combined with magnification also enhances the detection and characterisation of EGC. Emerging evidence regarding AI-assisted endoscopy demonstrates promising diagnostic accuracy for CAG, GIM, and early neoplasia, with improved lesion detection and reduced miss rates in several studies. However, limitations relating to external validation, generalisability, and integration into routine practice remain. Continued advances in optical imaging, structured training, and AI-supported diagnostics are likely to play an increasingly important role in improving early gastric cancer detection and surveillance outcomes worldwide.

records.title: The influence of chronic exercise intervention on the executive function of children with neurodevelopmental disorders: a meta-analysis.

content.title: The influence of chronic exercise intervention on the executive function of children with neurodevelopmental disorders: a meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

This meta-analysis examined whether chronic exercise interventions can improve executive function in children with neurodevelopmental disorders and aimed to identify the conditions under which these benefits are most pronounced. Although the review was framed within the broader category of neurodevelopmental disorders, the available randomized controlled evidence was mainly concentrated on attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Therefore, the findings should be interpreted primarily in relation to these two diagnostic groups rather than the full spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders.

Methods

A systematic search of six major databases was conducted to identify randomized controlled trials examining the effects of chronic exercise interventions on executive function in children with neurodevelopmental disorders. Thirteen randomized controlled trials involving 527 children were included, comprising 10 studies on children with ADHD and 3 studies on children with ASD. Executive function outcomes were synthesized across three core domains: inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility. Effect sizes were pooled using a random-effects model, and subgroup analyses were performed according to exercise type, intervention duration, exercise intensity, diagnostic subtype, and control condition.

Results

The pooled results showed that chronic exercise produced a moderate overall improvement in executive function. Among the three executive function domains, the largest effect was observed for inhibitory control, followed by a smaller but significant improvement in working memory. Cognitive flexibility also showed a small but statistically significant benefit after harmonization of outcome direction. Subgroup analyses indicated that intervention effects varied across exercise type, duration, intensity, diagnostic subtype, and control condition. In particular, closed-skill exercise appeared to produce more stable benefits for inhibitory control and working memory. Longer interventions were more favorable for improving inhibitory control, while moderate-to-higher intensity exercise showed greater promise for working memory.

Discussion

These findings suggest that chronic exercise may be a promising and accessible non-pharmacological approach for supporting executive function in children with ADHD and ASD. The results further indicate that exercise should not be regarded as a uniform intervention for executive function, because its effects differ across cognitive subdomains and intervention characteristics. Conceptually, this study advances the field by moving beyond the general question of whether exercise is effective and instead clarifies how, for whom, and for which aspects of executive function exercise may be most beneficial. However, the findings should be interpreted with caution because of substantial between-study heterogeneity and the limited number of trials included in several subgroup analyses.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/search, identifier CRD420261329177.

records.title: Distributed Artificial Intelligence for IoT Security: A Structured Review.

content.title: Distributed Artificial Intelligence for IoT Security: A Structured Review.
content.abstract: The expansion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has increased the complexity of securing distributed systems against growing threats to data security, privacy, and reliability. Conventional centralised cybersecurity methods are often insufficient for environments characterised by scale, heterogeneity, and dynamic behaviour. This paper presents a structured review of Distributed Artificial Intelligence (DAI) for IoT security, focusing on how local, cooperative intelligence can support intrusion detection, anomaly recognition, secure data processing, and collaborative defence. We synthesise the current literature on Federated Learning (FL), Multi-Agent Systems, and related approaches, highlighting their benefits, limitations, and practical deployment constraints. Particular attention is given to critical infrastructure contexts, where resilience is essential for operational continuity and public safety. The review concludes by outlining key gaps and future research directions for DAI-enabled IoT security.

records.title: Is plant-based protein supplementation as effective as whey protein? A systematic review and meta-analysis in untrained adults undergoing resistance training.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Is plant-based protein supplementation as effective as whey protein? A systematic review and meta-analysis in untrained adults undergoing resistance training.
content.abstract:
Background

Dietary protein supplements are commonly consumed to support increases in lean body mass among healthy adults engaged in resistance training (RT). Although whey protein has been extensively investigated, plant-based protein supplements have emerged as a viable alternative for individuals who avoid animal-derived products.

Methods

The present study aims to evaluate, through a systematic review and meta-analysis, the effects of plant-based versus whey protein supplementation on body composition in untrained adults (18-59 years) undergoing RT, using Dual-Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry (DEXA). The systematic review was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 checklist and was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251145410). Searches were conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect, identifying 5 studies that met the inclusion criteria for qualitative synthesis and meta-analysis.

Results

When combined with RT, both plant-based and whey protein supplementation were associated with improvements in lean body mass (LBM) and body fat mass (BFM), with no significant between-group differences observed.

Conclusions

Thus, soy- and pea-based protein supplements may support favorable body composition changes in adults initiating RT and could be considered practical nutritional options for individuals seeking alternatives to whey protein. Regarding chia-based protein, the available evidence is currently limited to a single study that did not demonstrate significant changes in lean body mass; therefore, firm conclusions regarding its efficacy cannot be drawn at this time.

records.title: Lower-Body Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations in Response to Concurrent Training in Trained Young Males.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Lower-Body Strength and Hypertrophy Adaptations in Response to Concurrent Training in Trained Young Males.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Gomes, M, Costa, M, Pezarat-Correia, P, and Mendonca, GV. Lower-body strength and hypertrophy adaptations in response to concurrent training in trained young males. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study examined the interference effect of concurrent training (CT) on maximal and explosive strength and muscle morphology in trained young males. Thirty subjects were randomly assigned to endurance training (E), resistance training (R), or CT for 11 weeks. The intervention comprised 2 mesocycles: weeks 1-5 emphasizing maximal strength, and weeks 6-11 targeting explosive strength. Assessments were conducted at baseline, mid-training, and post-training, and included leg-press maximal voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC), rate of force development (RFD), countermovement jump kinetics, and vastus lateralis cross-sectional area and pennation angle. Maximal voluntary isometric contraction increased only in the R group (18.4 ± 10.2%, p = 0.015). Peak RFD improved in both R (31.8 ± 23.2%) and CT (23.1 ± 27.9%), although with distinct time courses: R improved progressively across both mesocycles, whereas CT improved only during the second. Early-phase RFD (0-50 ms) increased in the R group from mid-training onward, whereas the CT group improved only from mid- to post-training (38.3 ± 40.4%, p = 0.021), accompanied by greater quadriceps electromyographic activity (p < 0.05). No changes in RFD were observed in E during training. Countermovement jump positive impulse improved in both R (12.7 ± 9.0%) and CT (8.8 ± 8.3%, p < 0.05), with no evidence of interference in jump-related explosive performance. Cross-sectional area increased in both R (17.0 ± 13.0%) and CT (8.8 ± 9.4%, p < 0.05). Pennation angle increased in CT (10.1 ± 12.9%) and R (18.6 ± 15.1%). These findings indicate that, although CT may limit MVIC development and delay early-phase RFD adaptations, it does not hinder explosive performance when resistance training is oriented toward rapid-strength development. Thus, CT can be effectively implemented in trained individuals when resistance training is periodized to emphasize neural-driven explosive or hypertrophy-related adaptations.

records.title: Effects of In-Season Contrast Strength Training on Jump Performance and Sprint Ability in Female Field Hockey Players.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Effects of In-Season Contrast Strength Training on Jump Performance and Sprint Ability in Female Field Hockey Players.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Chilingirian-Padrón, R, Álvarez-Yates, T, and García-García, O. Effects of in-season contrast strength training on jump performance and sprint ability in female field hockey players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of a 6-week in-season contrast strength training program incorporating sport-specific tasks on neuromuscular performance in sub-elite female field hockey players. Twenty-five athletes completed a pre-post single-cohort intervention integrated into their regular team schedule. Each session consisted of 3 sequential blocks: (a) a high-load strength exercise targeting maximal strength or hypertrophy (70-85% 1 repetition maximum [1RM]); (b) a biomechanically related explosive action performed at low load (∼30% 1RM) and high execution velocity; and (c) a high-speed sport-specific task. Jump performance was assessed using bilateral and unilateral countermovement jumps (CMJs) and free arm CMJ, whereas sprint ability was evaluated through 10- and 20-m sprints. A mixed-model repeated-measures analysis of variance was used to determine the effects of the intervention, with Time (Pre, Post) as within-subject factor and Playing Position (defenders, midfielders, forwards) as between-subject factor, with the level of significance set at p ≤ 0.05. Significant improvements were observed in all jump and sprint assessments: jump performance increased by 5.7-29.6%, whereas sprint ability improved by 1.6-1.9%. These findings indicate that 6 weeks of contrast strength training incorporating high-speed sports-specific tasks performed during the competitive season elicited meaningful improvements in stretch-shortening cycle-related jump performance and sprint ability in sub-elite female field hockey players.

records.title: Comparison of Functional and Traditional Strength and Power Training on U19 Soccer Players During Offseason in Norway: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Comparison of Functional and Traditional Strength and Power Training on U19 Soccer Players During Offseason in Norway: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Engberg Treu Lassen, L, Kersting, UG, and Pessoto Hirata, R. Comparison of functional and traditional strength and power training on U19 soccer players during off-season in Norway: A randomized controlled trial. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Functional training emphasizes multiplanar, soccer-specific movement patterns requiring body control, whereas traditional resistance training focuses on maximal force production through stable, bilateral lifts. Although both approaches are common in soccer physical preparation, their relative effects on soccer-specific performance remain uncertain. This study compared the effects of functional vs. traditional strength training on performance outcomes during the offseason in U19 male players. Thirty-three Norwegian players were randomly allocated to a functional training group (FTG, n = 11), a traditional training group (TTG, n = 11), or a control group (CG, n = 11) using stratified, concealed allocation. During the first 4 weeks, all groups completed 2 weekly soccer sessions; FTG and TTG additionally completed 2 supervised 70-minute strength sessions per week. In the final 4 weeks, FTG and TTG continued the twice-weekly strength training, whereas CG ceased organized training. Functional training group performed unilateral, multiplanar free-weight exercises, while TTG performed bilateral, uniplanar machine-based exercises. The primary outcome was technical soccer performance, with mobility, dynamic balance, sprint speed, change of direction, and vertical jump as secondary outcomes. Both FTG and TTG improved Loughborough Soccer Shooting Test (LSST) performance compared with CG (FTG: -0.43 seconds, p = 0.003, d = 1.62; TTG: -0.50 seconds, p < 0.001, d = 1.88). Traditional training group also increased body mass compared with the CG (2.20 kg, p = 0.002, d = 1.65). Functional and traditional strength training produced comparable improvements in LSST time. These findings highlight training dose response and support individualized off-season programs integrating physical preparation with sport-specific demands.

records.title: Effects of Prolonged Combined Aerobic and Strength Training on Movement Velocities During a Strength Loading Bout: Targeting Same Versus Separate Muscle Groups.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Effects of Prolonged Combined Aerobic and Strength Training on Movement Velocities During a Strength Loading Bout: Targeting Same Versus Separate Muscle Groups.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Feuerbacher, JF, Jacobs, MW, Dragutinovic, B, Rehbein, P, and Schumann, M. Effects of prolonged combined aerobic and strength training on movement velocities during a strength loading bout: targeting same versus separate muscle groups. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Combined aerobic and strength training may impair explosive strength performance, especially when targeting the same muscle groups. This study aimed to assess the effects of prolonged combined aerobic and strength training on movement velocities and velocity loss during a strength loading bout when the aerobic and strength training target the same vs. separate muscle groups. Thirty-two men participated in a 12-week intervention, divided into 3 groups: (a) LHLS (lower-body high-intensity interval training (HIIT) and strength training), (b) LHUS (lower-body HIIT and upper-body strength training), and (c) LSUS (lower- and upper-body strength training). Changes in the area under the mean propulsive velocity (MPV) and velocity-loss curves during strength loadings were analyzed pre- and postintervention. Squat performance was compared between LHLS and LSUS, while bench press performance was compared between LHUS and LSUS. The level of significance was set at ρ ≤ 0.05. During bench press loading, no statistically significant main effects for group ( p = 0.225), for timepoint ( p = 0.170), nor group × timepoint ( p = 0.943) were observed for MPV. In squat loading, a statistically significant main effect for timepoint was found ( p = 0.020), with a decrease in MPV for LHLS postintervention ( p = 0.006). The interaction between group and timepoint was not statistically significant ( p = 0.083). No statistically significant main effects for group ( p = 0.110, p = 0.076), for timepoint ( p = 0.590, p = 0.244), nor group × timepoint ( p = 0.626, p = 0.239) were observed for velocity loss in either bench press or squat loading. These findings suggest that explosive strength performance may be more susceptible to interference when aerobic and strength training target the same, rather than different, muscle groups.

records.title: The effects of a 4-week protein overfeeding protocol on body composition and influence of FTO genotype in exercise-trained men and women.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: The effects of a 4-week protein overfeeding protocol on body composition and influence of FTO genotype in exercise-trained men and women.
content.abstract:
Background

High-protein diets have consistently been associated with favorable changes in body composition in both sedentary and exercise-trained populations. Despite abundant evidence supporting protein intakes above the recommended dietary allowance (RDA) for active individuals, the effects of deliberate protein overfeeding, particularly in those already consuming adequate protein, remain incompletely characterized. The primary purpose of this study was to examine the effects of a 4-week protein overfeeding protocol on body composition in exercise-trained men and women. The secondary purpose was to determine whether body composition adaptations differed by FTO rs9939609 genotype.

Methods

Fifty-six exercise-trained men and women (age: 22.40 ± 5.78 years; body mass: 75.47 ± 14.98 kg; BMI: 24.52 ± 3.50 kg/m2; resistance training: 5.12 ± 3.35 h/week) were enrolled in a 4-week dietary intervention. Participants were instructed to increase their daily protein intake by approximately 20% above baseline while maintaining habitual training. Body composition was assessed pre- and post-intervention using a multi-frequency bioelectrical impedance device (InBody® 270). Dietary intake was self-monitored via MyFitnessPal®. Thirty-five participants completed both pre- and post-testing assessments and constituted the primary analysis. Linear regression models adjusted for baseline values indicated that FTO genotype was not a significant predictor of body composition changes (p > 0.05).

Results

Protein intake trended toward a significant increase over the 4-week period (pre: 146 ± 66 g/day vs. post: 164 ± 79 g/day; p = 0.053), representing an approximate 12% increase. Total energy intake, carbohydrate, and fat intake did not significantly change. Lean body mass increased significantly (pre: 59.95 ± 14.14 kg vs. post: 60.62 ± 14.42 kg; p = 0.005; Cohen's d = 0.31) and total body water increased significantly (pre: 43.85 ± 10.35 L vs. post: 44.34 ± 10.55 L; p = 0.005). Fat mass (p = 0.424), body fat percentage (p = 0.149), and total body mass (p = 0.09) did not significantly change.

Conclusions

A 4-week modest protein overfeeding protocol in exercise-trained men and women was associated with a significant increase in lean body mass and total body water without concomitant increases in fat mass. These adaptations were not modified by FTO rs9939609 genotype. These findings support the contention that higher protein intakes do not promote fat accretion and may facilitate improvements in body composition in trained individuals.

records.title: Effectiveness of Pelvic Floor Muscle Training in Women Soccer Players and Its Relationship With Quality of Life and Pelvic Floor Muscle Strength: A Randomized Controlled Pilot Study.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Effectiveness of Pelvic Floor Muscle Training in Women Soccer Players and Its Relationship With Quality of Life and Pelvic Floor Muscle Strength: A Randomized Controlled Pilot Study.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Sebastian-Rico, JM, Muñoz-Fernández, MJ, Martínez-Aranda, LM, Calvo-Lluch, Á, and Ortega-Becerra, M. Effectiveness of pelvic floor muscle training in women soccer players and its relationship with quality of life and pelvic floor muscle strength: a randomized controlled pilot study. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study investigated the effects of a 6-week pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) program on muscle strength, function, and the prevalence of related dysfunctions in professional female soccer players using a randomized controlled pilot study design. Twenty nulliparous professional soccer players from the Spanish professional league (2024-2025 season) were randomly assigned to an experimental group (n = 12) or a control group (n = 8). Assessments included anthropometric data, validated questionnaires (International Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire-Short Form and Broome Pelvic Muscle Self-Efficacy Scale), clinical interviews, and physical examination using the PERFECT method and manometry. The intervention consisted of a 6-week supervised PFMT program (4 sessions/week, 30 minutes each) progressed through 4 phases: education, proprioception, strengthening, and functional integration. Results showed significant group × time interactions for pelvic floor self-efficacy (Broome Pelvic Muscle Self-Efficacy Scale), with scores in the PFMT group increasing by 48.8 and 59.6% (p < 0.05), representing large between-group effect sizes (d = 0.91-1.26). Pelvic floor muscle performance increased by 122.4% in the intervention group (d = 1.25), whereas no meaningful changes were observed in the control group. No adverse events were reported. In conclusion, a 6-week supervised PFMT program is an effective and safe intervention for professional female soccer players, significantly improving muscle function and self-efficacy. These findings support the integration of PFMT for both therapeutic and preventive purposes in elite, high-impact sports environments.

records.title: Exploratory serum renal biomarker and eGFR responses to high-protein diets during resistance versus concurrent training in resistance-trained men.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Exploratory serum renal biomarker and eGFR responses to high-protein diets during resistance versus concurrent training in resistance-trained men.
content.abstract:
Background

High protein intake is common among resistance-trained athletes, but its association with renal biomarkers across different exercise modalities remains uncertain. This study investigated whether consuming a high-protein diet (3.2 g·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹) during 16 weeks of resistance training (RT) or concurrent training (CT) affects renal biomarkers and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) in resistance-trained men.

Methods

Forty-eight resistance-trained men (26 ± 6 years; BMI 25.6 ± 2.9 kg·m⁻²) were randomized to 16 weeks of RT or CT (4 sessions·wk⁻¹) while consuming either 1.6 or 3.2 g·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹ of protein in a 2 × 2 factorial design. Forty-four participants with complete pre- and post-intervention data were analyzed. Fasting blood samples were assessed for blood urea nitrogen (BUN), BUN/creatinine ratio, cystatin C, and eGFR calculated using the CKD-EPI creatinine (2021), cystatin C (2012), and creatinine-cystatin C (2021) equations. Within-group changes were evaluated using paired t-tests, and factorial effects were assessed using linear mixed-effects models (Time × Training × Protein).

Results

No statistically significant Time × Protein or Time × Training × Protein interactions were detected for any renal biomarker or eGFR estimate (all p ≥ 0.182). No significant within-group changes occurred in the 1.6 g·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹ groups (all p > 0.05). In both 3.2 g·kg⁻¹·d⁻¹ groups, BUN and cystatin C increased (all p ≤ 0.017), while eGFR estimates decreased (all p ≤ 0.009). The BUN/creatinine ratio remained unchanged (p ≥ 0.614). However, these within-group findings were descriptive because the corresponding interaction effects were not statistically significant.

Conclusions

In resistance-trained men, 16 weeks of high protein intake did not produce statistically detectable differences in renal biomarker or eGFR changes compared with moderate protein intake, irrespective of training modality. Although modest increases in BUN and cystatin C and small decreases in eGFR estimates were observed within the high-protein groups, these findings were not supported by significant factorial interactions. The limited sample size precludes excluding clinically meaningful differences, warranting further investigation in larger studies.

records.title: Performance and Physiological Responses to Strength Training Programs in Elite Judo Athletes.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Performance and Physiological Responses to Strength Training Programs in Elite Judo Athletes.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Campos, BT, Rodrigues, JGdS, Cal Abad, CC, Bachi, ALL, dos Santos, CMM, Tritto, AC, Kons, RL, Penna, EM, and Prado, LS. Performance and physiological responses to strength training programs in elite judo athletes. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study compared the effects of 2 short-term strength training models, block planning (BP) and undulating planning (UP), on performance, physiological, and perceptual responses in elite judo athletes. We hypothesized that BP would induce greater physiological strain due to the concentration of training stimuli. Eighteen judokas (14 men and 4 women) were randomly assigned to BP (n = 9) or UP (n = 9) for 4 weeks, performing 6 weekly strength sessions alongside technical-tactical training. Performance outcomes included countermovement jump (CMJ), muscle power (back squat and bent-over row), and the Special Judo Fitness Test (SJFT). Monitoring variables included internal load, heart rate variability (HRV), and well-being, while physiological markers included creatine kinase, tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and cortisol. Data were analyzed using 2-way repeated-measures ANOVA (p < 0.05). Both groups improved SJFT performance (p < 0.01), with no between-group differences. Block planning increased lower-limb peak power (p = 0.01; d = 0.90), whereas UP showed no meaningful change. Upper-limb power and CMJ did not change in either group. Internal load showed different temporal patterns between models. Block planning presented higher HRVcv values (p = 0.04), indicating greater autonomic perturbation. Creatine kinase and TNF-α increased over time in both groups (p ≤ 0.05), while cortisol showed an interaction without clear post hoc differences. In conclusion, BP improved lower-limb power but increased physiological strain, whereas UP elicited similar judo-specific improvements with lower recovery demands. These findings highlight the importance of training organization for balancing performance and recovery in elite judo athletes.

records.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: diets for body weight reduction.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: diets for body weight reduction.
content.abstract: The International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) has developed an official position on diets for body weight reduction. This critical analysis of the literature is intended to provide a scientific foundation for practitioners, coaches, and trainees regarding the effects of the major diet types in adults who are generally healthy, physically active, and/or athletic, while drawing from clinical research in those with overweight/obesity, when relevant. This position stand does not address acute dehydration-based weight cutting, pharmacotherapy (i.e. GLP-1RAs), or bariatric surgery. The following 15 points constitute the Position Statement of the Society; the Research Committee has approved them. 1) Diets for body weight reduction can be broadly categorized by the magnitude of the energy deficit, linearity of the deficit, and macronutrient composition. These factors need to be tailored to individual preferences, tolerances, and goals.2) Very-low-energy diets (<800 kcal/day) and low-energy diets (800-1200  kcal/day) produce greater short-term weight loss but lack long-term advantages over less aggressive energy restrictions, such as calorie-controlled diets. These aggressive diets may increase lean mass loss, although adequate protein intake and resistance training may mitigate this risk. Caution is warranted about insufficiencies in vitamins, minerals, fiber, and other nutrients.3) The evidence at-large shows a lack of differential effects between intermittent fasting variants (alternate-day fasting, time-restricted eating, and twice-weekly fasting) and continuous energy restriction on anthropometric outcomes, although macronutrient quality plays an independent role in optimizing body composition and metabolic health.4) Intra-day meal frequency (as opposed to total daily nutrition) does not tend to crucially influence body weight and body fat reduction. Meal frequency may be individualized flexibly; no lower or upper limits can universally be prescribed to optimize outcomes. However, in physically active and athletic populations, distributing protein across at least three protein-rich meals (or eating occasions) per day may optimize lean mass retention and performance during sustained energy deficits.5) Resistance training and sufficient protein intake are indispensable mitigators of lean mass loss in a sustained caloric deficit, regardless of the diet type or variant. Total daily protein is of primary importance; specific distribution of the constituent doses is a secondary concern.6) For the general population, a daily protein intake of 1.2-1.6 g/kg BW is appropriate for supporting total body weight and fat loss, physical activity, and imparting benefits to musculoskeletal and cardiometabolic health.7) Daily protein intakes ranging 1.6-2.2 g/kg BW combined with resistance training may optimize muscle anabolism, while higher intakes of 1.9-3.2 g/kg BW can maximize lean mass retention in lean, resistance-trained individuals sustaining hypocaloric conditions.8) The dietary carbohydrate‒fat proportion can be individualized to personal preference for the goal of weight loss, since the range of ketogenic to low-fat diets performs similarly.9) Ketogenic diets are effective at bodyweight and body fat reduction, but they also tend to decrease fat-free mass to a greater degree than higher-carbohydrate comparators, particularly in shorter trials where glycogen and total body water shifts can influence estimates.10) Adaptations to weight loss can be physical, physiological, and/or behavioral, and converge toward reducing energy expenditure to fulfill the body's drive toward neutralizing disruptions to homeostasis imposed by the caloric deficit.11) Adaptive thermogenesis is a reduction in resting energy expenditure beyond that predicted by changes in body composition. It can occur in response to hypocaloric conditions and weight loss, but it is not an inevitable response, and it may attenuate substantially upon attainment of weight stability.12) Metabolic adaptations that reduce energy expenditure, including adaptive thermogenesis, and impair gut microbial diversity, can often be attenuated by strategic dietary and exercise programming that foster nutrient-absorption and partitioning, and metabolic flexibility.13) A multitude of tactics can be implemented to manage and overcome plateaus. However, plateaus are also opportunities/cues to practice maintaining progress made thus far (the ultimate goal is the maintenance of a plateau).14) Guidance from an interdisciplinary team of health professionals while maintaining social support is recommended for successful weight management.15) Learning how to prepare home-cooked meals (and plan meals ahead of time through the day) puts dieters in control of their nutritional fate - and in a better position to succeed in managing their body weight and body composition.

records.title: Do Putative Human Reticulospinal Tract Properties Adapt Following Short-Term Isometric Resistance Training?
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Do Putative Human Reticulospinal Tract Properties Adapt Following Short-Term Isometric Resistance Training?
content.abstract:
Purpose

The primary purpose of this study was to investigate whether isometric resistance training (RT) leads to reticulospinal tract (RST) adaptations.

Methods

A "RT group" of 30 healthy adults completed 4 weeks (15 sessions) of volume-matched unilateral elbow flexion RT involving high (32 repetitions/session at 70% maximal voluntary torque [MVT]) or low (64 repetitions/session at 35%MVT) loads. An additional 15 participants served as controls (CON group). Pre- and post-test MVT, RST properties (RST gain ratio derived from the StartReact assessment; startling auditory stimulus-conditioned/control motor evoked potential [MEP] ratio; and startling stimulus-conditioned/control cervicomedullary MEP [CMEP] ratio), CST excitability and intracortical inhibition properties (in response to transcranial magnetic stimulation) were assessed.

Results

MVT increased more in the RT group (+12.8%; n = 30) vs. CON group (-4.3%; n = 15; group (2) × time (2), p = 0.001). However, changes in RST properties assessed using a series of indirect measures did not differ between the RT group (-1.4% to 6.6%; n = 30) and CON group (-4.5% to 10.5%; n = 15; group (2) × time (2), 0.352 ≤ p ≤ 0.834).

Conclusions

RST adaptations within a sample of healthy young men and women, assessed using various indirect measurement approaches, did not occur following only 4 weeks of isometric elbow flexion RT. These findings add to the currently limited scientific evidence from short-term human RT intervention studies available to inform the use of RT for healthy individuals or patients primarily targeting the development of RST function.

records.title: Beyond the Hangover: Associations Between Binge Drinking, Health, and Performance in Young Adult Resistance-Trained Females.
records.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

content.title: Beyond the Hangover: Associations Between Binge Drinking, Health, and Performance in Young Adult Resistance-Trained Females.
content.abstract:
Purpose

The present study aimed to evaluate associations between resistance training and binge drinking in relation to musculoskeletal composition, physical fitness, cognitive function, and psychological wellness in young adult females.

Methods

Participants were categorized into four groups: sedentary low alcohol consumers (SL; n=12), sedentary binge drinkers (SB; n=12), resistance-trained low alcohol consumers (RTL; n=12), and resistance-trained binge drinkers (RTB; n=12). Measurements included body composition via DEXA scan, muscle quality via ultrasonography, and insulin sensitivity via oral glucose tolerance test. Physical performance was assessed using maximum chair stand power, vertical jump, broad jump, knee extensor torque, grip strength, and push-ups to failure. Tests and questionnaires were used to assess cognitive function and psychological wellness.

Results

Resistance-trained females had lower body fat than sedentary females (RTL = 29.28±4.27%; RTB = 29.03±3.67%; SL = 37.18±5.32%; SB = 34.83±3.54%; p<0.05), and RTL had more fat-free mass than SL and SB (RTL = 48.31±5.81 kg; SL = 38.08±6.59 kg; SB = 40.37±6.05 kg; both p<0.05). There were no differences between RTL and RTB in bone mineral density, muscle quality, or physical performance. RTL outperformed SL and SB on vertical jump (both p<0.05) while RTB outperformed SL and SB on broad jump. RTL had lower fasting blood glucose than RTB (88.92±12.09 mg/dL and 103.17 ± 10.21 mg/dL, respectively; p=0.008), and lower postprandial blood glucose than all groups (RTL = 103.83±19.82 mg/dL; RTB = 137.58±21.54 mg/dL; SL = 148.50±44.60 mg/dL; SB = 139.25±14.49 mg/dL; all p<0.05).

Conclusions

The results suggest that ≥1 year of binge drinking is associated with poorer metabolic health without differences in performance in young females. Further, frequent RT may mitigate the effects of binge drinking on body composition.

records.title: Multiple Sessions of Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation Combined With Squat Training Improve Lower-Limb Maximum Strength in Healthy Adult Men.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Multiple Sessions of Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation Combined With Squat Training Improve Lower-Limb Maximum Strength in Healthy Adult Men.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Yan, X, Zuo, Z, Nitsche, MA, Zhang, X, and Qi, F. Multiple sessions of transcranial direct current stimulation combined with squat training improve lower-limb maximum strength in healthy adult men. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-This study aimed to investigate the effects of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) combined with Squat training (ST) on lower-limb maximum strength in healthy adult men. Sixty men (age: 21.6 ± 2.1 years, height: 177.5 ± 5.3 cm, body mass: 73.1 ± 7.4 kg) were randomly assigned to 4 groups (tDCS + ST group, sham tDCS + ST group, tDCS + rest group, sham tDCS + rest group). The 6-week intervention program was implemented with biweekly sessions, totaling 12 treatment sessions, each separated by a minimum 48-hour interval. After the tDCS intervention, the ST groups performed squat exercises while the tDCS + rest and sham tDCS + rest groups sat quietly for 30 minutes. Lower-limb maximal muscle strength was measured at 4 distinct time points: preintervention (T0), 24 hours post-third week intervention (T1), 24 hours post-sixth week final session (T2), and 1 week post-entire intervention completion (T3). Key evaluation metrics were measured, including 1 repetition maximum (1RM) squat, knee extensor and flexor peak torque, and rectus femoris cross-sectional area (CSA). Significant improvements in 1RM, knee extensor strength, and nondominant rectus femoris CSA were observed in both tDCS + ST and sham tDCS + ST groups compared with the sham tDCS-only group (p < 0.05). No differences in knee strength, 1RM, or rectus femoris CSA were observed between the tDCS + rest and sham tDCS + rest groups. The results indicate that anodal tDCS combined with ST does not yield additional training benefits on lower-limb maximal strength in healthy adults when compared with ST alone.

records.title: Do Athletes Lose Soleus Strength Over the Course of a Season? Longitudinal Monitoring of Seated Plantar Flexion Maximum Voluntary Contraction Strength and Factors That Affect It in Australian Football Players.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: Do Athletes Lose Soleus Strength Over the Course of a Season? Longitudinal Monitoring of Seated Plantar Flexion Maximum Voluntary Contraction Strength and Factors That Affect It in Australian Football Players.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Green, B, Pizzari, T, Schache, AG, Rio, EK, Evans, SCS, Cooper, S, and Murphy, MC. Do athletes lose soleus strength over the course of a season? Longitudinal monitoring of seated plantar flexion maximum voluntary contraction strength and factors that affect it in Australian football players. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-The calf muscles are critical to dynamic lower-limb function in sports but are susceptible to injury. Despite its role in performance and injury, research has not evaluated soleus strength changes over the course of a season, or factors affecting it. Flexed-knee maximum plantar flexion strength was longitudinally monitored in state-league Australian footballers (2 Western Australian and 1 Victorian team) across 1-season at timepoints: preseason (T0), early in-season (T1), late in-season (T2). Generalized estimating equations evaluated strength outcomes over time (absolute, relative, asymmetry). Intrinsic factors (e.g., age, sex, injury history, sport exposure history, calf-focused resistance training) were analyzed to determine longitudinal associations with strength. Forty-one athletes (32 male, 9 female) were monitored across 210 strength measurements from T0 to T2. Absolute (T0 = 121.7 ± 27 kg; T1 = 135.2 ± 27.3 kg; T2 = 135.8 ± 25.9 kg) and relative (T0 = 1.51 ± 0.28 body mass [BM]; T1 = 1.69 ± 0.27 BM, T2 = 1.75 ± 0.26 BM) strength demonstrated longitudinal change (absolute: β = 19.33 kg, relative: β = 0.24 BM; p < 0.001). Reduced strength was associated with a recent calf injury history (relative and absolute: p < 0.001) and older age (p = 0.03). Lower strength (absolute: β = -23.53 kg, relative: β = -0.22 BM; p < 0.05) and larger asymmetry (β = 8.13 kg, p = 0.01) were detected in female athletes. Athletes can be expected to improve and maintain soleus capacity across seasonal periods. Athlete age, calf injury history, and sex can affect strength longitudinally. These findings may guide individualized prevention, performance, and postinjury benchmarking.

records.title: An Automated Blood Flow Restriction Device Is Reliable, but Not Valid, for Determining Lower Limb Occlusion Pressure in Resistance-trained Adults.
records.publisher: Journal of strength and conditioning research

content.title: An Automated Blood Flow Restriction Device Is Reliable, but Not Valid, for Determining Lower Limb Occlusion Pressure in Resistance-trained Adults.
content.abstract:
Abstract

Lang, D, Fallo, X, and Bennett, H. An automated blood flow restriction device is reliable, but not valid, for determining lower limb occlusion pressure in resistance-trained adults. J Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000-000, 2026-Blood flow restriction (BFR) exercise can improve strength, hypertrophy, and aerobic performance. Accurate limb occlusion pressure (LOP) assessment is essential for safe prescription. The AirBands is a novel automated BFR device that estimates LOP using integrated sensors, making LOP assessment easier. However, its validity and reliability are not well established in resistance-trained individuals. This study evaluated the concurrent validity of the AirBands compared with a handheld Doppler ultrasound for lower limb LOP, and its test-retest reliability, in resistance-trained adults. Twenty-six resistance-trained adults (14 males, 12 females; 24.2 ± 4.7 years) participated. For validity, LOP was measured using AirBands and Doppler in randomized order, using the same cuff. For reliability, automated LOP was measured twice, 10 minutes apart. Agreement was assessed using Bland-Altman limits of agreement and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC). No significant difference was observed between manual (231.7 ± 17.8 mm Hg) and automated (230.8 ± 38.3 mm Hg) LOP (mean difference -0.8 mm Hg; p = 0.928), although validity ICC was poor (0.236, 95% confidence interval [CI] = -0.293 to 0.641). Bland-Altman analysis indicated proportional bias, with overestimation at lower values and underestimation at higher values. Reliability showed no significant difference between test 1 (243.0 ± 37.5 mm Hg) and test 2 (242.3 ± 40.5 mm Hg) (mean difference 1.0 mm Hg; p = 0.816) and good reliability (ICC = 0.862, 95% CI = 0.715 to 0.936). AirBands demonstrates good test-retest reliability but poor concurrent validity vs. Doppler ultrasound. Clinicians should confirm automated values using a Doppler ultrasound before prescribing BFR.

records.title: Effects of extremely low-volume high-intensity interval training combined with iron supplementation versus iron supplementation alone on postural control in young women with iron deficiency anemia: a randomized controlled trial.
records.publisher: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition

content.title: Effects of extremely low-volume high-intensity interval training combined with iron supplementation versus iron supplementation alone on postural control in young women with iron deficiency anemia: a randomized controlled trial.
content.abstract:
Background

Recent research revealed postural control deterioration in young women with Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA). To address this postural deficit, it is crucial to develop intervention strategies for postural rehabilitation in these individuals. This study aimed to explore the effect of 8-week extremely low-volume high-intensity interval training (HIIT) based on plyometric exercises combined with iron supplementation versus simple iron treatment on postural control of young women with IDA.

Methods

This randomized controlled trial enrolled young women with IDA aged 18-25 years, who were randomly assigned to a training group (TG; n = 16) or a non-training group (NTG; n = 17). All participants received oral iron supplementation (ferrous sulfate, 494.5 mg/day, administered as 247.25 mg twice daily), while the TG additionally completed an 8-week extremely low-volume HIIT program based on plyometric exercises. Hemoglobin (Hb) and serum ferritin concentrations were assessed, alongside muscle endurance, reaction time performance, and postural control. Muscle endurance was evaluated using the Killy test, reaction time performance using an online simple reaction time test, and postural control using a stabilometric platform under bipodal and semi-tandem stance conditions. Postural assessments were conducted with eyes open (EO) and eyes closed (EC) on firm and foam surfaces. All outcomes were measured at baseline and 72 h after the final intervention session.

Results

After the 8-week intervention, this study demonstrated significant improvements across both groups, irrespective of the intervention. However, TG showed significantly greater post-intervention improvements than NTG in Hb concentration (P = 0.042), muscle endurance (P < 0.001), and postural control. Superior postural control in TG was observed during a bipedal stance on a foam surface (EO: P = 0.001); EC: P = 0.035), as well as during semi-tandem stance on a firm surface (EO: P = 0.015; EC: P = 0.040) and on a foam surface (EO: P = 0.019; EC: P = 0.003), compared to the NTG. With a Bonferroni-adjusted significance threshold for multiple comparisons (α = 0.00625), between-group differences in postural control remained significant for bipedal foam EO (P = 0.001) and semi-tandem foam EC (P = 0.003).

Conclusions

The study showed that women with IDA improved their postural performance regardless of the intervention used. However, an 8-week program of extremely low-volume HIIT combined with plyometric exercises and iron supplementation had a more beneficial effect compared to traditional iron therapy.
